The study of quantum systems under the influence of time-symmetric external forces is relevant for multiple applications, including interaction with time-varying environments and optical materials. We have created an experimentally achievable, non-equilibrium steady state that showcases persistent, time-periodic coherence within a quantum bit system. Consistent with our experimental data, we have developed a theoretical model based on a time-dependent Liouville equation and developed an efficiently computable method for calculating its steady states. Our approach allows us to accurately capture the quantum bit's persistent behavior and provides insights that can be applied to broader scenarios.

This investigation focuses on biharmonic hypersurfaces within a Euclidean space. We examine cases where two semi-symmetric connections yield compatible harmonic maps, and subsequently analyze special configurations involving multiple Comonov operators, before ultimately investigating instances where surfaces exhibit equality between their associated energies.

Let id(p/q) denote the set of integer modules x for which the polynomial (x^m + x^n + 1)/(x^p + x^p + 1) is reducible, where p/q is a reduced positive fraction and n, n, n are distinct multiples of p/q. Previous research has established a link between (p/q) and the logarithmic reduction of x modulo (x^p + x^n + 1). Building upon this connection, our work proves a formula for calculating the logarithmic reduction, thereby providing an inductive method to determine the structure of modules id(p/q) based on reducing the numerator or denominator of the fraction p/q. Specifically, these calculations can be represented using combinatorial sequences such as binomial coefficients, falling factorials, and Bell numbers.

Our research extends the traditional "axion dark photon" concept to a more complex scenario, called the "axion dark photon substance," by incorporating two additional components: sterile neutrinos that interact weakly and a new type of particle formed from the combination of axions and photons. We focus on the properties of this hypothetical particle substance, particularly its two types of particles that move at the speed of light. We name this concept the "axion-stereile-neutrino substance," and suggest that it might explain certain characteristics of dark matter, including its apparent lack of self-interaction. We also discuss how this particle substance could have a significant impact on the formation of structures in the universe and its small-scale distribution patterns, and how it might be detectable through its gravitational effects on visible matter.

The LAMOST time-domain science exploration (TDES) project has recently begun,  
utilizing four $K$2 plates to expand the TDES database to 3.6-0.96$\mu$m,  
with a goal of amassing 10 million observations over the course of 10 years,  
with 6 nights allocated each month. These observations are conducted every  
3-10 seconds, every other night, in a time series format. In order to compare  
and complement this data with the LAMPOST spectral template, we analyzed a subset  
of the TDES data, comparing it to synthetic spectra and finding a high level of  
consistency (S/N$\sim$100) between the two. We also explored the potential for  
studying stellar surface behaviors, such as spot rotation, and found evidence of  
this in two solar analogs ($\sim$10 d and $\sim$2 d periodicities). However, we were  
unable to find the same evidence in two other asymptotic giant branch stars. We  
also used the TDES data to estimate the ages, masses, and radii of three solar  
like stars and two red giants, with a high level of precision (better than 10\%),  
with a significant improvement expected as the TDES project continues to grow.

When using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in three-dimensional (3D) analysis, there is a risk that the model may focus excessively on high-frequency details or background elements, similar to overfitting. This phenomenon has led researchers to question the consistency of CNNs' ability to identify high-level small objects or tissue boundaries in three-dimensional (3D) applications. In this paper, we contend that edge detection capabilities of CNNs must be explicitly trained and regulated in three-dimensional (3D) settings. A novel framework called Edge-Gated CNNs has been devised to enhance the edge sensitivity of a model by integrating an additional edge-aware network, which is trained with a supplementary edge-aware loss, while the main network is modified to incorporate the edge-sensitive information through integration and retraining with an edge-aware gate loss. For experimentation, we utilized the SynthSeg dataset consisting of simulated data and the HPB and KiTS19 datasets containing real medical images. Results demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms existing edge-sensitive baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on all three datasets when applied to automatic segmentation of liver and adjacent organs in CT images.

MongoDB's popularity has surged with more than 20,000 deployments on PyPI, and it has become a preferred database for web applications due to its ease of use and high performance. However, as a document-oriented database with multi-version concurrency control lacking transactional integrity, users may encounter issues of data inconsistency and unpredictability in its behavior. To address this limitation, we introduced a transactional integrity validation framework for MongoDB called TIM, which can be seamlessly integrated as an application layer into existing MongoDB deployments without affecting the database or requiring code changes in web applications. Essentially, TIM acts as a transparent wrapper that ensures the reliability and consistency of data by providing a robust transactional framework.

Tim operations function as a virtual transactional layer over MongoDB's existing collection-based operations, allowing them to be executed on single documents. Unlike traditional two-phase protocols, TIM employs a novel hybrid approach that combines aspects of both to improve performance and reduce latency. To further enhance its efficiency, TIM uses a virtual conflict resolution mechanism called TIM-DOCA, which draws from MongoDB's underlying engine to minimize the overhead associated with its transactional operations.

Benchmarking and real-world system evaluations demonstrate that TIM can achieve a significant improvement in system throughput, achieving up to 10 times greater performance than MongoDB's existing collection-based operations while maintaining low latency within 1.5 times the original levels. To open up the possibility of exploring different conflict resolution mechanisms, TIM provides a modular plugin system for easy experimentation and

We demonstrate the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric polynomials for any tree, an property previously known only for specific polynomial identities related to Catalan numbers. Furthermore, we establish an explicit connection between the coefficients of these polynomials and the entries of the inverse matrix with positive integers from the Kostka-Tao-Stanley combinatorial perspective. This connection resolves an open query regarding the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric polynomial for any Dyck path, providing a particular formula that satisfies the necessary condition.

To tackle the issue of hasty and inaccurate human judgments, we develop a hasty and unreliable huffman tree that summarizes the legal fines as penal suggestions, thereby assessing a person's ability to impose penalties.

Our research indicates that both the tree and a human expert agree with each other's opinions, but diverge significantly from average hasty reactions to legal penalties, leading us to classify entities capable of negotiating fair penalties as penal agents.

A custom-built HintsWorld game has been constructed to train a neural network-based agent using the Hindsight Summary-Sampling (HSS) process, which combines hindsight summarization and hasty re-labeling to evaluate and adjust opinions on penal suggestions.

Our findings reveal that the HSS process allows the H-assessor to outperform both average hasty reactions and human experts in terms of preference consistency with the penal agent in terms of penal suggestions.

The success of deep learning techniques in medical imaging analysis relies on high-quality annotated data. However, many publicly available datasets are assembled using manual labels from a diverse group of medical professionals, and some of these labels may be of questionable accuracy due to inherent bias. To address this issue, our research develops a framework for detecting and quantifying this type of baised detection in medical image collections. We propose using a simple network to identify anomalies in detection patterns and demonstrate its effectiveness through both real-world expertise and controlled simulations. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric for measuring bias and apply our detection framework to a dataset of brain tumor images, identifying and mitigating detected biases.

Complex systems composed of interconnected components are prevalent in various fields including biology, sociology, and technology. These types of networks often contain particularly densely connected regions or "motifs," and researchers have developed a statistical measure called curvature to characterize their structure. By extending the concept of curvature, a specific feature known as hidden geometry has emerged, offering significant advantages in comprehending the underlying structure of these intricate assemblies. A notable application of this framework involved analyzing triangular interactions in magnetic nanoassemblies, where it helped reveal how certain connections influence overall behavior by promoting a spin-reversal phenomenon. Furthermore, a dynamic extension of curvature was created to analyze how certain time-dependent forces affect conjugated systems, allowing for an examination of wave propagation patterns within these structures. Overall, the research has established hidden geometry as a crucial aspect of understanding complex systems with interconnected components.

The inner heliosphere is shaped by the Sun's influence as it travels through the galaxy. As the Sun's magnetic fields and solar winds interact with each other and with ancient remnants from supernovae, cosmic radiation is regulated before reaching Earth. Our research uses data from the Parker Solar Probe to examine how energy moves within the solar winds near the Sun. As the probe approached the Sun for the first time, we used real-time observations to analyze how different types of energy were being transferred as we moved through various plasma conditions. By comparing magnetic fields, solar winds, and temperature to computer simulations, we found that turbulence plays a key role in controlling the flow of energy. In some areas, heat from the Sun's magnetic fields was more significant, while in others, the interaction between magnetic fields and plasma was the main factor. By studying these processes, we can gain insights into how cosmic radiation reaches Earth and shapes habitable zones around other stars.

Speech-emotion recognition is often compromised by data variability due to its reliance on large datasets. Few-shot learning techniques have been attempted to address this issue, but they typically neglect the issue of data distribution. To bridge this gap, our proposed approach adapts multiple deep reinforcement learning policies to transfer knowledge from large datasets to large and smallemotional datasets, leveraging similarities across different domains. In our evaluation, a convolutional neural network extracts audio features and a max-entropy reinforcement learning module adapts the emotion probabilities. Furthermore, a gradient reversal layer combats negative transfer and enhances cross-domain adaptation. Our comprehensive approach, incorporating these components, is asserted to overcome the limitations of solely adapting rewards. Experimental results validate the efficacy of our proposed method.

This paper examines the four-layer Aurivillius perovskite Bi5FeTi3O15 and its doped variants using nuclear forward scattering, under high hydrostatic pressure. Measurements were conducted at 4.3K to investigate the magnetic properties of the Fe sublattice. Applying high pressure causes a shift in the hyperfine magnetic field towards lower values, with the rate of change significantly influenced by the Ni dopant. Specifically, the rate of change is approximately 25 T/kbar for the Ni-doped sample, in contrast to about 10 T/kbar for the undoped sample. This variation in the magnetic field's response to pressure suggests a variegated magnetic structure that adapts to high pressure conditions. Furthermore, an increase in electrical conductivity with high pressure was observed, with a variegated conductivity of approximately 10^-5 times an optical frequency scale, or 10^-12 s, indicating the presence of multiple coexisting conductivity mechanisms within the sample.

The shortest route problem on a graph with edge cost variability is complex, especially when applying it to free-flight planning. Previous research has developed models and algorithms for this purpose, but their success depends on solving a large-scale graph problem. We investigated the impact of solving an imperfect routing problem on the errors resulting from the assumption of independent and normally distributed node costs. Our findings indicate that ignoring the interdependence of costs may lead to substantial cost underestimation in problems with numerous alternatives, and we suggest an algorithm to estimate the true cost of the route selected by this interdependent cost model.

A significant effort has been made to understand the effects of a powerful, outward-moving shockwave on a nearby object, which has numerous implications in astrophysics and physics, particularly in the study of pulsar blasts and gamma-ray explosions. A model consisting of an expanding universe with a spherical void at its center has been utilized to examine these effects, considering the impact of a strong shockwave on an object behind it. A numerical algorithm has been developed to solve the associated hydrodynamic equations using a fifth-order method known as HC5-DS, which has been implemented in a public online tool, Hydrodynamics in an Expanding Cosmos. This model allows users to observe the behavior of an object behind a powerful shockwave as it propagates through different layers of the surrounding medium in an expanding universe. The results reveal that the object experiences intense compression, significantly altering its size and shape, which has direct implications for laboratory experiments aimed at studying high-pressure phenomena. Users can also explore these effects through the interactive HC-DS hydrodynamics simulator available online.

Teaching materials for particle physics frequently rely on low-resolution visuals that can hinder understanding. You can improve the accessibility of your content by using high-quality images and ensuring they are easily readable by all students. Recent research presents a precise measurement of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ decay rate as a function of $D_s^{-}$ mass, which can serve as a valuable update to existing standard model benchmarks. A comprehensive study was conducted with the aim of determining the impact of various theoretical and experimental factors, such as how the $D_s^{-}$ is identified and selected, and how well the momentum of the $\mu^{+}$ is understood. The results of this study show that the $B_s^0$ form factor at specific $D_s^{-}$ mass values is within the range of 0.304^{+0.018}_{-0.016} (statistics)^{+0.010}_{-0.009} (systematic). Further analysis revealed that the $B_s^0$ form factor at the $D_s^{-}$ mass resonance peak is 0.304^{+0.018}_{-0.016} (statistics)^{+0.012}_{-0.011} (systematic). These measurements can be utilized to determine the branching fraction and average angular Wightman-C

In this research, we establish a connection between polynomial solutions to the Schrödinger equation and the vanishing of monodromy in the associated potential. Specifically, it is shown that the existence of such solutions for an infinite number of energy levels directly implies the absence of monodromy in the potential, again, within a specific class of potentials. A key result is proven where, for a Lagrangian quantum mechanical system with a polynomial potential, discrete, non-equidistant energy levels are found, and local coordinate transformations are shown to yield a single-valued, polynomial transformation of the action-angle variables, thereby demonstrating the absence of monodromy. This finding is then generalized to a class of Schrödinger operators, and it is observed that the property of having a spectrum of descending monic Hermite polynomials and the associated monodromy-free superpotential is shared by operators that form an isospectral family, and this relationship holds for both linear and non-linear Lagrangian systems.

When detaching a tape from a surface, a phenomenon known as unpeeling occurs, which can be studied by analyzing the intermittent snapping sounds it produces. These sounds result from the formation and sudden expansion of cracks within the tape. By examining the dynamics of this process in detail, researchers have discovered that a hidden orderlies the chaotic appearance of the crackle sound, and this order follows a universal pattern. Specifically, the relationship between the speeds at which different parts of the tape separate from each other can be visualized as a clear boundary, and systems with similar physical properties share this underlying structure.

The discovery of superconductivity by B.D. Josephson in 1962 and its subsequent demonstration in 1963 laid the groundwork for superconducting electronics, with Josephson junctions serving as the fundamental building blocks. However, the initial applications of this phenomenon were hindered by limited scalability, until the rise of CMOS technology in the 1980s spurred interest in quantum computing and other advanced fields, reigniting research in superconducting electronics. This historical overview traces the evolution of superconducting electronics, with a particular emphasis on recent advancements in 2D materials research. Given that this field is still in its nascent stages, a Josephson junction phase error analysis based on atomic-scale dimensions and material properties is suggested as a viable next step. Furthermore, suggesting using 2D materials for fabricating SQUIDs and junctions to minimize dispersion and increase critical currents, thus serving as potential design blueprints, is suggested.

Theories incorporating a symmetric derivative tensor on the dark sector's one-form field have been analyzed from multiple perspectives, specifically in terms of fundamental theory, physical properties, and application in cosmological models with finite temperature. Our research reveals that an "non-abelian Einstein-Aether" theory, when formulated with three type-disfixed coefficients, demonstrates excellent agreement with observed cosmological parameters. This agreement is maintained even after accounting for a conventional matter component, and closely matches current Planck constraints. Furthermore, our work extends previous work by incorporating non-abelian effects and examining finite temperature impacts. Additionally, our analysis indicates that an "non-abelian Einstein-Aether" theory may be connected to a Lagrangian containing a double-covariant curvature term and a symmetric derivative tensor defined on gluon fields. This connection becomes apparent in the high-temperature regime, influencing the critical temperature at which the early universe transitions from a hadron universe to a quark-gluon plasma universe.

The price of a collateralized European option under active delta hedging is determined by a modified Black-Scholes equation that accounts for transaction costs, option price changes, and the options gamma values, assuming a constant spread in option price and steady delta hedging transactions at a power of the stock price, we derive a general solution to the modified equation; specifically, if stock dividend exists the analytical equation is also derived.

Delineate the process of solving a nonlinear elasticity equation with a highly contrasted, periodically varying Young's modulus that adheres to a specific periodicity pattern. The modulus is defined by its values in a solid and a fluid component of the material, with an overall volume fraction of the solid component being significantly less than one. The study aims to determine under what conditions a simplified description can be applied to the deformation process, either as a fluid dynamics problem or as a modified elasticity equation in the solid component only. A key focus is placed on understanding the conditions in which the deformation can be characterized within a lower-dimensional subspace perpendicular to the variation of the material's structure.

We analyzed tidal structures in early-type galaxies using a flux-based percentage method in a wide area of the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Camera's 143 square degrees. Our deep and wide-field survey will significantly enhance our statistical understanding of galaxy mergers, especially for fainter galaxies beyond the local range. Our initial analysis of 550K early-type galaxies revealed that tidal features are more prevalent in brighter galaxies and those with higher masses. Tidal structures in this study are likely the result of recent mergers with at least medium-sized galaxies. Based on the characteristics of tidal features, our results on galaxy merger rates in 0.8 < z < 1.4 show that elevated rates are mainly found in brighter galaxies, while in dimmer galaxies, overlapping error bars render the tidal structures more equal across different magnitudes.

A crucial factor in shaping a society's long-term success is creating opportunities for its youth to thrive and contribute to the community. To examine how various policy decisions impact the transmission of opportunities across generations, a novel model was developed. This model's innovative approach lies in its ability to measure 'advancement transmission' - a unified metric that captures the probability of parents providing their children with access to high-value roles within the community. The model reveals that financial incentives play a crucial role in maximizing intergenerational opportunity transmission, with the results indicating a disparity where children of individuals from wealthy backgrounds are three times more likely to end up in wealthy positions compared to children from low-income families. Furthermore, simulations based on these models have shown potential for improving societal outcomes through targeted support programs for younger individuals from disadvantaged backgrounds, with minimal negative effects on overall opportunity transmission rates.

The cutting-edge field of high-power lasers is advancing rapidly, with significant breakthroughs already achieved and many opportunities for even more innovative developments. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of high-power laser technology, encompassing its fundamental building blocks and complex systems that utilize these lasers for various applications such as atomic research, high-speed communications, and material processing. This inset provides the necessary background for even non-experts to grasp the basic principles behind high-power laser systems and their intricate workings.

We prove that for $1\ll \varepsilon \ll 1 \ll p \ll \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$, any subset of $\ell_p$ with $\varepsilon$-isometric dimension $k$ contains a $(k-1)$-isometric subset of dimension at most $k-1$.

A method known as brightness scanning, which involves moving a beam across a target to determine the beam's properties, such as its shape and movement, is commonly used. These determinations are typically made by analyzing how a target's response changes when the beam moves in predefined patterns, usually requiring the target to be much smaller than the beam. However, a new approach, which we propose, allows the target to be much larger than the beam by using a technique called fill-mode brightness scanning. This approach, which we demonstrate via both theory and experimentation, involves calculating the changes in a target's total emitted light, rather than the emitted light in a specific direction, to obtain the standard metrics needed to analyze a beam. These metrics include the effective area, displacement, and movement caused by a particle beam.

This paper aims to enhance the robustness of optimization techniques in networked systems by developing a distributed optimization method that is resilient to malicious attacks. A new algorithm is proposed, which takes into consideration both the efficiency and resilience of traditional methods, enabling it to counteract arbitrarily manipulated data and restore normal operation after the attack has been detected and localized. Furthermore, theoretical analysis demonstrates that the algorithm can achieve an optimal convergence rate of O(1/k) in the absence of attacks. Moreover, the algorithm's performance in terms of communication cost and convergence speed in response to attacks is analyzed, with further details explored through numerical simulations. These results indicate that, although optimal convergence may not be achieved, near-optimal rates with improved accuracy and reduced impact magnitude can be attained.

The current systematic uncertainties affecting precision measurements of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) are primarily instrument-related and may mask the potential of the experiments to reach their sensitivity limits set by physics. To address this issue in the future, high-precision simulations that incorporate realistic models of the instrument's performance are needed before observing real data. These simulations are crucial for evaluating and detecting how the instrument-related systematic errors could impact the final results and parameter constraints, particularly in experiments focused on cosmic neutrino properties and primordial gravitational wave detection. This paper outlines the methodology and features of the Simulations for 4-year CMB Surveys (s4cmb) code, a state-of-the-art simulation tool being used in the Big Bang Heritage in Four Experiments project, and demonstrates its capability to pinpoint the origin of the instrument-related systematic errors and evaluate their impact on the final results and parameter constraints, specifically in the case of the Large-Angle Atmospheric Internal Radiometer and Absolute Calibration of the Background with four years of data.

Indispensable modern NLP systems are largely based on word-based neural networks trained with a loss minimization approach, with success heavily reliant on utilizing large language models pre-trained on vast datasets. Though widely studied from various perspectives, the inner workings of these models remain unclear. To address this study focuses on one specific aspect of pre-training tasks - word arrangement, with a narrowed examination of BART's performance in restoring word sequences, with inputs consisting of three words in different orders. Through numerous experiments with numerous scenarios this study reveals that (i) utilizing models with an reduced number of training parameters yields similar results to utilizing models with numerous parameters; (ii) models utilizing large datasets perform better than models utilizing smaller datasets, with a notable finding that models utilizing vastly smaller datasets can achieve comparable results to utilizing large-scale BART models; (iii) both bigram co-occurrence and context window size play a crucial role in model performance. To gain insight into pre-trained models this study proposes utilizing a novel model with comparable optimal pre-training requirements but with interpretable components. Additionally this study suggests that (r) the context window size influences models' understanding of semantic relationships; (a) models' decisions are not solely reliant on statistical frequencies but also influenced by semantic contexts; (b) pre-trained models may be susceptible to bias induced by data distributions.

The rapid dissemination of convincing video and audio deepfakes necessitates the immediate development of efficient detection methodologies. A crucial aspect in deepfake identification lies in pinpointing the traces left by an attacker during the creation process. Our research reveals that certain patterns, left unchanged during the manipulation process, can serve as effective features for deepfake detection. This study employs needle detection as a means of extracting these patterns and introduces an innovative approach known as the Cross-Seawing Transformer, which builds a swapping network that extracts features and fuses them to enhance feature richness. Furthermore, our model incorporates a unique strategy called MD-Blocking to prevent overfitting and prevent leakage of identity information. By integrating these components, we establish a novel deep learning architecture for deepfake detection, which demonstrates superior performance on prominent datasets including Celeb-DF, OASIS, and Formals. Our results reveal a remarkable accuracy of 94.83% on the Celeb-DF dataset, 97.41% on the OASIS dataset, and 93.57% macro macro-average accuracy on the Formals dataset. Additionally, our research reveals that the proposed method exhibits robust resistance to various attack methods and exhibits reduced sensitivity to threshold tuning.

Researchers have introduced the concept of stochastic block models (SBMs) to represent the structure of code graphs, using two matrices to define the degree-degree and adjacency relationships. By employing this framework, they analyzed the decoding process of LDPC codes over a binary erasure channel (BEC) through a pseudo-likelihood equation, which can be solved via fixed-point iteration. They derived an analytical method involving the use of SBM entropy and derivative matrices, which is particularly useful for quasisparse degree-degree distributions where traditional approaches fail. This method was demonstrated with various examples, including regular, irregular, and hybrid LDPC codes of different sizes and rates. Additionally, they explored the connection between the binary erasure threshold (BET) and the degree-degree distribution, which may have implications for code design. Their proposed analytical approach is less computationally expensive than simulation methods and provides clearer insights into the behavior of the BEC threshold based on the code's degree-degree distribution.

A novel approach to mitigate the impact of phase randomization techniques on the performance of quantum key distribution systems has been investigated. This technique, which involves introducing random phase variations into decoy photons to counteract the effectiveness of the B92 with dimension reduction protocol, had previously been theoretically proposed. In this study, we move beyond theoretical limitations by examining the feasibility of this technique in a practical application, and present findings that support its viability. Our experiments, conducted using a cloned attack as a benchmark, demonstrate minimal additional performance losses of up to 0.04 dB/km compared to the standard DDPS system when employing partially randomized phase variations, and an achievable sensitivity of -145.42 km when using completely random phase variations. These findings imply that users can anticipate only negligible impacts on system distance performance when implementing this technique and support its feasibility in enhancing the security of quantum key distribution systems.

This paper outlines key concepts for a self-managing and eco-friendly 5G mobile network, leveraging a range of modern and adaptable central network control methods. We delve into various central optimization techniques used to enhance MIMO resource allocation, energy efficiency, and overall network performance. Particular attention is given to investigating supply chain strategies, green energy applications, and sustainable hardware acquisition practices. Latest advancements in central optimization, such as deep learning and statistical modeling, are also discussed. Furthermore, we highlight critical research gaps in the area of central network management processes.

In the late 1800s, Menger rekindled interest in geometry by examining the foundations of geometry in a general setting. Building on Riemann's work, he devised an abstract framework for studying distances between points in a space. A decade later, he expanded upon this by considering angles between paths within a geometric space. Although various definitions of angle exist, the precise formulation of certain angle conditions, specifically the circular and four angles conditions, had yet to be rigorously addressed. This study provides a precise definition of angle between paths in a space, contributing to the resolution of the four angles problem and offering a potential solution to the circular condition. Furthermore, it establishes relationships between specific angles and certain properties of the space in question.

We derive bounds for the distance between lattice points and the shortest vector in a ranked lattice within a number field, extending Baker's work on linear forms. This generalization allows us to expand the existing bound, which we apply to enhance the shortest vector bound of Drinfeld-Vladu on the cache size of algebraic curves.

We've developed a novel dual sensor 1-d hybrid femtosecond-picosecond rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy system that utilizes an ultrashort and a short laser pulse respectively for obtaining precise and well-resolved spectra in frequency domains. By combining the spectra advantages of CARS and DRAMS, our system is capable of simultaneously measuring temperature, pressure, and gas composition via analysis of a solitary sample. Data was collected by exchanging an ultrashort laser pulse and a short laser pulse at different frequencies and then processed to eliminate the effect of the Raman gain profile and the Raman shift of the Raman active gas. The results show our dual sensor system is capable of simultaneously and accurately (within 5%) measuring temperature, pressure, and gas composition in a highly turbulent flow environment without the influence of the Raman gain profile and the Raman shift, and is capable of providing highly accurate measurements (within 3%) when the sensor structures are optimized and the samples are appropriately selected.

The traditional view of planetary formation involves dust clumping together under gravity within calm regions of a planetoid disk. However, the disk's dynamics, driven by outward forces, are not adequately addressed in this theory. A new model is now examined that addresses this issue by considering the development of regions stillness within the disk itself. This model involves the interaction between magnetic fields and electric currents that ultimately sets the stage for planet formation by determining the thermal patterns in the disk and influencing the efficiency with which dust converts into solid planets.

Observations from the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider indicate that in heavy ion collisions, the path of charged particles often forms an elliptical shape along the direction of motion, and this pattern is typically aligned with the direction of motion. In contrast, circular patterns are less common. These neutral patterns, however, can produce dc electric currents due to the directional nature of their alignment. Our calculations reveal pattern-induced dc electric currents to be significant, particularly for neutral patterns when considering their cross-sectional area. On the other hand, dc electric currents resulting from an aligned pattern are so minimal that they can be disregarded. As such, pattern-induced momentum anisotropies are likely negligible and thus probably do not contribute to the formation of quasi-particles with aligned spins in heavy ion collisions.

We introduce two novel families of cluster algebras, each with its own set of initial variables. The first family, denoted as $\mathcal{A}_\mathfrak{t}$, aligns with the type of algebras first described by Gelfand, Retakh, and Karzerman. The second family, denoted as $\mathcal{A}_\mathfrak{c}$, corresponds to certain quantum Weyl algebras in specific cases. It is demonstrated that both families of cluster algebras are related to deformations of the universal enveloping module of a quantum enveloping algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$. Notably, $\mathcal{A}_\mathfrak{t}}$ and $\mathcal{A}_\mathfrak{c}$ are found to be isomorphic to their respective deformed versions of $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$, for both simply laced and non-simply laced affine Lie algebras, when viewed as modules over their respective underlying polynomial rings.

This research paper introduces a novel classification learning algorithm capable of adapting to image changes, often referred to as learning with graph transformations. To achieve this, we incorporated a distributionally robust optimization framework into a decentralized learning process. By representing the changes as a graph, we developed an adaptation rule that ensures the robustness of the decentralized model. The proposed algorithm DR-DSGD uses robust gradient descent updates in an asynchronous decentralized environment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through experiments conducted on the MNIST dataset using a change graph constructed from the digits' visual parts. The results show the ability of the algorithm to prevent performance declines in testing conditions that differ from the training change graph. Additionally, the proposed method provides theoretical convergence guarantees suitable for decentralized settings.

Computing simulations of hard-drives have been in existence since computers were first developed. Initially focused on magnetic tape units, researchers eventually shifted their attention to rigid and later hybrid drives as these technologies replaced the older ones. Several factors were considered in these simulations, including the characteristics of the hard-drive, various forms of disturbances, and algorithms used for data access. Despite numerous advancements in hard-drive design and data access algorithms over time, certain fundamental aspects have remained constant. To facilitate understanding of this complex evolution, we created a simplified model that captures the core principles of hard-drive operation and can be easily applied in teaching settings. To further facilitate this learning process, we also developed an interactive tool using Java Web Start technology.

Jet scale dependence is crucial for understanding jet production but difficult to measure due to large theoretical uncertainties. To address this issue, we calculated medium-modified jet spectra and yields with various inputs, including Gaussian fluctuations in temperature and nuclear PDFs like EPPS08 and nCT14, across a range of central collision energies from 2.76 TeV to 5.2 TeV. Our simulations were validated against recent jet data from the LHC showing a varying nuclear modification factor at different energies. However, varying the nuclear PDFs or nuclear scaling violations alone did not match the observed energy dependence. Instead, jet scale effects combined with nuclear PDFs were found to be essential for replicating the jet data and nuclear scaling violations observed at various collision energies. This highlights the significance of jet scale effects and current nuclear PDF uncertainties in medium-modified jet production processes.

The Forsage cryptocurrency pyramid scheme, which operates through a smart contract on the Binance Smart Chain, is analyzed in this study. The blockchain's capability to facilitate randomized outcomes via hash functions, in contrast to the limited probabilistic capabilities of Turing-complete programming languages used in programming languages such as Solidity, is first explained. We then explain how Forsage utilized this feature to create a fair lottery system, incorporated into its pyramid scheme, for its top-level members. The complex way the pyramid scheme operates, meaning new members' contributions are solely beneficial to certain members depending on the timing of their transactions, is then discussed through a historical example and a mathematical simulation. Finally, the unexpected result that the project's supply of coins may run out before the majority of the participants recoup their initial investments, is demonstrated through a simulation taking into account the complex, non-Turing-compliant properties of the Forsage smart contract, is investigated.

The 10 most massive known bulge globular clusters are sufficient to constrain bulge formation models, yet there are numerous other sub-maximal mass clusters in the bulge region that could provide useful information. Our analysis uses the VISTA-VVV survey and near-infrared data compilation to systematically examine cluster mass, density, and dynamic stability. We identify nine clusters with high mass and integrity, including ANS 4, ANS 8, ANS 10, ANS 12, ANS 14, ANS 15, ANS 16, ANS 18, and ANS 19, that are suitable for further dynamic and photometric research to determine their underlying properties.

Using the effective field theory EWI, we refine our non-ab initio calculation of heavy quark influence in hadron-colider collisions for spin-1 final states. For processes like Drell-Yan, we demonstrate the factorization of cross-section into universal components representing the proton and the effective weak interaction matrix elements, enabling independent computation. While previous research demonstrated this for total and partial cross-sections, our work extends this to differential distributions and specifically examines rapidity distributions at the LHC for dimuon production with invariant masses exceeding 200 GeV. By including heavy quark contributions in proton and effectively including their emission during the weak interaction at the EWI matching scale, our calculations show excellent agreement with CMS data, often outperforming calculations that consider only standard perturbative corrections. For certain differential distributions, our calculations significantly reduce unexperimental uncertainties, thereby providing a more precise theoretical prediction. Furthermore, our formalism permits the inclusion of various non-perturbative effects, such as those from the proton's intrinsic quark distributions and the heavy quark's finite transverse momentum, which can be seamlessly integrated using the SOKA framework.

The accuracy of density functional theory is limited by the quality of the input parameters used within its tight-binding models. Recent research has focused on developing sophisticated, high-fidelity model Hamiltonians that could potentially replace more complex models like the time-dependent jellium model. A significant aspect of this work involved analyzing how the quality of these interactions changes based on the method employed to derive effective charges and hybridization matrix elements from first-principle calculations within the empirical pseudopotential method and the tight-binding approach. Using a silicon supercell as a case study, our team demonstrated that slight variations in these methods lead to noticeable differences in predicted electronic properties such as density, polarizability, and optical gaps, which deviate from density functional theory calculations and experimental results. According to our simulations, these discrepancies arise from the sensitivity of these models to the method used, rather than inherent flaws in the modeling approach. Consequently, our team suggests that model parameters should be consistently obtained through the same procedure within a given calculation to minimize these differences. Additionally, this study suggests that simplifying model Hamiltonians may be sufficient for obtaining reliable results, as long as their parameters are carefully selected.

In this research, a new variant of the holographic multi-scale entangle entangle annealing state that is invariant under symmetry transformations was examined. By starting with a known invariant state under the $SO(d)$ group and then applying a set of local unitary operations in an inverse sequence, we obtained an approximate code state that maintains fidelity with its target state within a specific bound. We discovered that for a bond dimension that scales according to a power law, the fidelity failure rate also follows a similar pattern. A change of variables within the geometry of the dual gravity theory renders the scaling dimension of the operator relevant in an inflection point, thereby demonstrating that our proposed state can detect and correct a significant variety of non-local disturbances. Furthermore, we investigated the behavior of the code in the limit as the dimension $d$ approaches its maximum value, finding evidence of a threshold phenomenon in the case of $d=3$ and $d>3$. Our results also show that the coexistence of invariance and efficient scaling is attainable, while revealing discrepancies between the scaling behaviors of the holographic and tensor network models for certain operators.

A theoretical analysis of retinal isomerization is performed in a molecular junction in this study, by using sp electrons and modifying bond parameters to facilitate retinal's transition from one isomeric state to another. Retinal-like systems are found to exhibit an extraordinary sensitivity to minor changes in external voltage in a series circuit, as they mostly remain in a single isomeric state and occasionally undergo rapid switches between states in response to specific voltage fluctuations. These results indicate that retinal-like molecules have the potential for use in designing novel memory and sensing components that operate based on their photoisomerization properties.

In this study, various deep learning models including Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Multi-Layer Perceptron and Convolutional Neural Network are evaluated to enhance Business Process Model and Sequence Diagram generation. We examine Process Mining concepts, compare the performance of these models using precise metrics and demonstrate their limitations in producing high-quality processes. Our results indicate that the deep learning approaches generate processes with lower precision and recall values when assessed through Process Mining metrics. However, combining these models with Process Mining techniques yields improved outcomes. Unfortunately, current Business Process models like Model and Sequence Diagram generation models require real-time data processing, which significantly slows down their efficiency. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach utilizing pre-trained models for more effective process prediction. Our experiments show that this hybrid model outperforms traditional approaches in terms of precision, recall and F-measure but still generates processes with suboptimal quality. Due to the complexity of Business Process models, our work focuses on simple processes and leaves room for future research to explore more advanced scenarios.

Social media platforms can be invaluable in responding to disasters by providing immediate insights into the affected areas and aiding relief efforts. Analyzing tweets enabled us to examine the effects of the 2020 Izmir earthquake in Turkey and support organizations seeking to assist the victims. By examining Twitter user posts, we identified key regions heavily affected by the quake and ranked local businesses by the frequency of mentions in the days following the event. This approach allowed us to pinpoint establishments that may have been damaged or closed as a result of the disaster, potentially providing relief teams with crucial information to prioritize them for inspections.

We delve into the non-triviality and boundary characteristics of Gelfand-Shilov areas $\Sigma^{\sigma,\tau}\subset\mathbb R^n$. Our research brings out key insights into their structure, leading to significant findings regarding their size and composition. Notably, we demonstrate that these areas have measurable properties and a rich internal makeup. This in turn enables an examination of the impact they have on the behavior of certain mathematical functions and the potential development of specific types of linear transformations. We have characterized the boundary of these areas using a specific mathematical condition, identified their essential composition, and established that they have a rich internal makeup. These findings enable an exploration of the behavior of certain mathematical functions and the potential development of specific types of linear transformations. Notably, we demonstrate that these areas support a specific type of mathematical function and have a rich internal makeup. This in turn enables an examination of the impact they have on the behavior of certain mathematical functions and the potential for significant insights into the composition of certain types of mathematical objects. AD Leo is a well-documented KH binary star system that has undergone multiple eruptions since its initial discovery in 1947. Researchers have since studied four of its eruptions in detail, but data on its ultraviolet spectrum during these events has been limited. This study presents an analysis of 11 available HST observations spanning from 1985 to 2015, during the eruption's peak in 1985. By calibrating the near-UV data and combining it with optical spectrum information, researchers were able to determine the characteristics of the erupting gas in 1985. This study reveals significant differences in the velocities of hydrogen emission between the 1985 and other post-chandrasekhar limit events, indicating a diverse range of ultraviolet velocities. Additionally, further research is needed to determine the link between ultraviolet and X-ray emissions in AD Leo.

Non-reciprocal devices are commonly found in the fields of magnetism, optics, and electronics. Owing to their ability to process signals directionally, these devices are also sensitive to changes in non-reciprocal parameters. This sensitivity enables the creation of sensitive detectors within periodic structures consisting of such devices. This research explores a periodic setup consisting of two coupled systems: non-reciprocal units in series with PT-symmetric pairs. Analyzing this setup through mathematical models demonstrates the preservation of transmission when it involves PT-symmetric pairs but breaks down with non-reciprocal units. This issue can be rectified by adding specific coupling strengths between adjacent units. Furthermore, this research delves into the interaction between PT-symmetry and coherent perfect absorption within this periodic setup, finding that CPL can be realized only when the external input signals are aligned in phase with one another under certain strong coupling conditions. These results provide a basis for developing highly sensitive detectors within periodic photonics networks and novel platforms to explore PT-symmetry-based interactions.

The primary method for studying large-scale networks involves analyzing their dynamics through mathematical models. Unfortunately, solving these models exactly becomes impractical for large networks, prompting researchers to focus on sparse networks and employ non-Markovian approaches for larger-scale assessments. Alternatively, logical dynamical models offer a practical solution by representing node states as binary variables and dynamics based on state transitions, which can be applied to networks of any size. Though these models are effective, their ability to capture complex interactions, including multi-node influences and self-interactions, is limited due to their binary nature. This study introduces a novel, non-intrusive technique for creating binary dynamical models that can incorporate complex two-way interactions, enabling an investigation into the models' landscape, stationary distributions, and dynamics on networks of any size. Our results demonstrate that these logical models can produce diverse patterns, including multistability, self-sustained oscillations, and damped decay, and our study reveals that network topologies can significantly impact model landscapes and dynamics, resulting in predictable oscillatory patterns for certain network structures.

We derive explicit mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of simple operators on top of a general time-reversed Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave function. These expressions can be applied to evaluate matrix elements on top of HFB configurations made up of single-quasiparticle excitations. For simple operators acting on individual particles, we employ a method known as "normal ordering," a technique used to rearrange the operators. This enables exact evaluation of matrix elements of single-quasiparticle operators and introduces a source of ambiguity, known as "pairing noise," in matrix elements of two-body operators. This pair of operators can lead to inaccuracies in matrix elements as a result of their non-commutative nature. This technique enables exact evaluation of matrix elements of single-quasiparticle operators, which can be exact for matrix elements of two-body operators, resulting in inaccuracies in matrix elements as a result of their non-commutative nature.

However, such method introduces a source of ambiguity, known as "pairing noise," in matrix elements of two-body operators. This arises due to the disorderly arrangement of operators leading to inaccuracies in matrix elements as a result of their non-commutative nature.
